To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the most variable type I collagen sequences in the three domesticates species, bovine, ovine and porcine, are not among those that have been used previously as species biomarkers, (ii) the most variable peptides are not among those with the highest relative abundance in the tissues investigated and (iii) the alpha 2(I)-chain is more variable than the alpha 1 chain, with no apparent functional significance.

the most variable type I collagen sites, as identified by LC-based methods, are not among the sites identified as species-specific biomarkers in PMF-based studies, and that intra-chain functional properties are not as important as inter-chain properties in determining sequence variation.
the most variable type I collagen peptides in cow, sheep and pig tissues can be detected by liquid chromatography-based tandem mass spectrometry, but not by peptide mass fingerprint analysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the application of mass spectrometry to the analysis of collagen sequences, and how the results of this research can be used to inform the development of future methods of taxonomic identification.

identifying the most variable sites in the collagen molecule, which can be used for species identification in archaeological specimens, and the advantages and limitations of each method for collagen identification.
the identification of collagen biomarkers for species differentiation, using both PMF and LC-based methods.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

both approaches can be used in conjunction to provide the most comprehensive and accurate species identification of collagen, with LC-based methods providing a greater degree of detail, but only when required.
the LC-based methods are not yet ready for routine use in collagen-based taxonomic identification and that further work is required to improve the publicly available collagen sequence database.

PMF analysis is still the most appropriate method to identify collagen from archaeological and palaeontology specimens, while LC-based proteomics is the more sensitive method for the identification of collagen in modern samples.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

PMF is the most appropriate method to use for initial species identification, with LC-based methods used only for confirmation of species identity, or for further in-depth analysis of specific collagen sites.
the LC-based methods are better at identifying the most variable collagen peptides, but are also more prone to false positive identifications.

the PMF method is the best approach for species identification, but the LC-based method can be used to further confirm the species identity, and to identify the most variable peptides in collagen, and thus the most suitable peptides for further investigation of sequence variation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
collagen is a highly variable protein, with a large number of potential biomarkers for species determination.
collagen sequence variation, as a biomarker for species identification, can only be fully appreciated when both PMF and LC-based methods are employed in tandem.
the use of PMF is still the most suitable method for species identification of collagen, with LC-based methods being reserved for further analysis of specific peptides of interest.
